sections.topic_sentence: The hard problem of building software with agents is simple to state: the tools are fast and the tools are unreliable.

sections.heading_text: What this book is about (and what it is not)
sections.topic_sentence: Not every programming task needs the machinery this book describes.

points.text: The first judgment an agentic engineer makes is whether a task needs governed autonomy at all, because some tasks a capable model completes in one pass.

sections.heading_text: The two modes
sections.topic_sentence: Start at the decision on the left.

points.text: Once a task's input and output are stated, the choice of mode forks on the work's size and difficulty.
One-shot scripting fits a small task that needs no subtle reasoning: specify the behavior once, take the single-pass result, skip the governance apparatus.

Supervised autonomy fits a hard or oversized task: rather than hand the agent the whole job, you supply four things — correctness conditions, sub-tasks, determinizing tools, and monitoring-and-intervention — in two groups, one shaping what gets built and one shaping how the building runs.
The four elements form the skeleton of supervised autonomy, and each later part of the book develops one of them.

sections.heading_text: Where the emphasis falls
sections.topic_sentence: This book is about both modes.

points.text: Telling the two modes apart is the first skill, and misjudging it either way is expensive: over-govern a one-shot task and you drown it in ceremony; under-govern a supervised one and you get plausible, subtly wrong output at unreadable scale.

How long a leash a task can run on depends on two things: how densely the model's training data covers the work, and how capable the model is at it — well-trodden work for a strong model can be described briefly and trusted far, edge work needs the reasoning broken into smaller checked steps.

The book's weight falls on supervised autonomy — building products whose quality needs exceed what a model can be trusted to do alone and whose size exceeds any context window — because that is the new, unwritten engineering.
Writing code is no longer the expensive part, so the book's premise is turning a fast code-fabricator into a production line.

sections.heading_text: The printer
sections.topic_sentence: A 3D printer will build almost anything you can imagine — a replacement gear, a prosthetic hand, a scale model of a building — out of nothing but spooled filament.

points.text: A 3D printer builds almost anything from spooled filament, limited only by material and imagination; it is the governing metaphor of the book because coding with an agent is far more like running a printer than people expect — and that difference is the difference between blaming the tool and blaming yourself.

sections.heading_text: An open-ended technology
sections.topic_sentence: A 3D printer is not just a machine.

points.text: A 3D printer is an open-ended technology, in the rare company of writing and the printing press: none arrives with a list of what to make, so people must invent the genres, and cheap production mints genres no predecessor could justify.

Generative AI is open-ended the same way, so the work is not only to run the machine but to work out which genres are worth producing and a method for each; this book takes one genre — production software, code whose named quality metrics each change traces back to.

The book's apparatus is not decoration but the price of any trustworthy software — name the properties that must hold, check them, tie every change to the property it moves; that price was always the same, and what changed is that agents drop its cost so the assurance once affordable only to a regulated few is now within nearly anyone's reach.

sections.heading_text: A picture is not enough
sections.topic_sentence: Everyone can sketch a piece of software.

points.text: Anyone can picture a piece of software, because the concept is easy to picture — but a picture is not a thing you can print.
A 3D printer given a photograph produces nothing; it needs a model of internal structure plus print notes, because there are a hundred ways to misprint a part that looked fine as a picture.

Software agents are the same: you cannot hand an agent only the picture of what you want; you must supply the detailed build instructions, and the quality of the result tracks the quality of those instructions.

sections.heading_text: Whose fault is it?
sections.topic_sentence: Here is the shift in posture the whole book turns on.

points.text: The posture the book turns on: an agent is not a foolproof stapler but a printer that builds only what its instructions describe, so when it produces the wrong thing the first suspect is the instructions, not the model.

In the author's experience every agent failure traced back to his own instructions: state-of-the-art models can build essentially anything one can envision so long as you can explain it, and that "so long as" is the whole job — a real, teachable engineering discipline.

That the printer builds anything you describe is both the promise and the danger: with no judgment behind it, it builds a wrong thing as fast and willingly as a right one, carrying you at full speed exactly where your instructions point.

Speed is not the danger but exposes it: hand the machine a doomed idea and it does not slow to warn you, it builds your mistake with the same tireless fidelity as your success, and which one comes out is the instructions, which are yours.

The book's running example is not a toy but a real shipped system — DocAble, the production accessibility-remediation tool — returned to in every later chapter so what the reader watches getting printed correctly is a system that actually shipped.

sections.heading_text: Everything is a loop
sections.topic_sentence: An agent does not run in a straight line — it runs in a loop, and the loop has a fixed shape.

points.text: An agent runs in a loop of fixed shape — input (the problem plus a notion of success), reasoning, action, output, folded back into the next input — and shaping that loop is loop engineering, of which nearly everything in the book is an instance.

Engineering a loop well starts with the metric, because the agent steers by it and does not know your goals; make progress measurable — deterministically, by a quantitative check, or by a rubric scoring a qualitative result — or the agent searches forever, never knowing when to stop.

The companion repository's orchestrator is a worked example of an engineered loop: it models the dispatch → work → land → tombstone lifecycle as an explicit reactive loop written down as a model the agent can read, rather than left implicit in the code — which is exactly the second idea.

sections.heading_text: Give it a model of the world

points.text: Vibe coding treats the program as an I/O device; engineering treats it as a system.

The difference between the two is not aesthetic but what counts as proof a change is good: the I/O device asks only whether the right thing came out this time, the system asks what must stay true across every input — and the fast, seductive I/O default is what turns a hundred thousand lines into a mess nobody can reason over.

The second piece is the model the agent reasons over: a sense of the environment — what happens when it pulls a lever, and what it is even allowed to do — which is itself an input, and supplying it tells the agent what kind of reasoning the situation calls for.

Writing the model down is not wasted breath because a foundation model is a probabilistic reasoning machine: probabilistic means it does not always do exactly what you want, reasoning machine means it genuinely reasons over real internal structure — so it reads what you write and reasons over it.

The most useful way to hold this is as a search: the agent is searching an enormous space — every place the answer might live, every configuration, every function that might implement the ask — far too large to sweep.

Structuring the loop and handing over a model conditions the probability distribution of the agent's behavior — biasing its search toward where the answer actually is; done well this moves the agent from failing the task to completing it, and completes already-solvable tasks in fewer tokens and less time.
A model earns its keep twice: it aims the search, and it shrinks what the agent must hold — which keeps the work from spilling the context window and churning.

The printer metaphor's honest break: a real 3D printer is deterministic — same G-code, same part — while this printer is probabilistic — the same prompt can yield different output — which is why we condition the agent's distribution rather than merely instruct it; the metaphor claims you get only what you describe, not that you get the identical thing twice.

preamble_points.text: Two ideas carry the rest of the book: all agent work is a loop, and an agent steers that loop well only when handed a model of the world it works in — engineering the loop and handing over the model, deliberately and every time, is the MAGE method.

sections.heading_text: The four layers
sections.topic_sentence: **At the bottom sits the foundation model.** It comes from a commercial vendor or an open-weight release, and it is a general language reasoner that can *induce* an understanding of your environment — but that induction is expensive, and it happens fresh every time.

points.text: At the bottom of the stack sits the foundation model, a general reasoner that induces an understanding of your environment fresh and expensively each time; the game at this layer is to spare that cost by telling it up front where to look — deterministically, softly, or a hybrid — because every stretch of reasoning you supply is one fewer step in the chain where a compounding error can enter.

The foundation layer rests on one claim — the model reasons rather than retrieving stored answers, building and causally intervening on an internal world representation (the Othello-GPT board-state result, generalized across settings) — so the job at this layer is to equip it to reason well by supplying the context, packaged as a skill, that starts its reasoning from your world instead of a guessed one.

On top of the model sits the agentic harness, which manages the context window — the fixed token budget whose overflow forces a lossy compaction — and holds two of the most useful mechanism points, sharply distinguished: a hook is something the agent has to do, a skill is something it can choose to do.

The harness carries two mechanism kinds: a skill is a soft mechanism — trigger criteria plus guidance, whose code half is a tool that lets the model take a deterministic action instead of guessing — while a hook is a hard mechanism, a deterministic program run before or after a harness action that can inspect and forbid it, giving authoritative control at the moment the agent acts.

Above the harness sits the engineering environment — the tools, conventions, and processes a team carries in its head — which for an agent must be written down because it has none by default, and which offers its own injection points: git hooks on every command (the classic being a pre-commit hook that moves a fast quality check as far left as it goes) and the CI pipeline's stages above them.

At the top sits the application — the product code itself, which carries governance of its own: models of how it should work, and static analyses that check the code against them; a static analysis here can make a whole class of mistake structurally impossible, as a ban-lint that routes all mutation of a format through one typed model does, enforced once at the seam and holding for every agent that touches the code.

sections.heading_text: Every layer is a place to steer
sections.topic_sentence: Read the stack as a list of opportunities, because that is what it is.

points.text: Read the stack as a list of injection opportunities: the harness banking a summary before a lossy compaction, the pre-commit hook catching a defect while its cause is still in-window, the CI failure turned into a message the agent can read — each layer is a place to help the model reconstruct less or catch a defect sooner.

The single goal under every layer never changes: prevent a bad choice and narrow the agent's search toward the choices you want — which matters because the context window cannot hold a serious system at once, so absent structure the model burns its window inducing the rules of the road, and every mechanism on the stack is a rule handed to it for free.

The mechanisms installed at these layers do not act in isolation — they run together, and two that touch the same thing at the same moment pull against each other and confuse the agent, so governing each layer is not enough; the interplay between mechanisms is its own problem.

The stack is where the book's two theses get their footing: a model handed to a layer enacts the Modeling Thesis, tying intent to implementation and shrinking what the agent holds in-window, while a hook or lint installed at a layer enacts the Alignment Thesis — and the two chapters that follow take one thesis each.

preamble_points.text: Governing an agent means conditioning where it searches, and there is no single place to reach in — the agent stack has four layers stacked on each other, each giving a different kind of grip, so every mechanism in the book is an instance of "pick a layer, inject a constraint."

sections.heading_text: Words are soft, code is verbose, a model is the sweet spot
sections.topic_sentence: Your first governance mechanism is the prompt, because the agent is a language model and words are how you talk to it.

points.text: The first governance mechanism is the prompt, but words are soft — ambiguous, and only pushed part-way down by documentation; that documentation suffices for a human team, which remembers and knows what matters, but not for agents, who are brilliant reasoners needing to be told exactly what to reason over.

Code is the opposite failure — perfectly precise but far too verbose to reason over in bulk — so what you want sits between the two: something accurate and unambiguous yet compact, and the word for that thing is a model.

A model, as physics already teaches (F = ma, y = mx + b), is not reality but a cheap, honest approximation you can actually reason over instead of wrestling the full dataset; software has its own such models, and UML — the famous 1990s attempt at a whole language of them — never took off, for the reason this chapter exists.

sections.heading_text: Why the models drifted — and why that changes now
sections.topic_sentence: The models are the map; the code is the territory.

points.text: The model is the map and the code the territory; the territory drifts as code changes, and keeping the map in sync by hand is expensive — with no single model capturing everything, teams either piled every concern into one unreadable mega-model or split into so many views that one code change meant updating ten diagrams, so they gave up and drew box diagrams.

A hand-maintained model rots the moment the person maintaining it stops — the new hire cannot tell whether the diagram describes the system or lies about it, and the first person to trust the stale map pays for the gap; that lived failure is why the practice fell out of favor everywhere but the industries where a mistake is catastrophic and the cost is justified.

Agents flip the calculation: they cannot reason over the code because there is too much of it, but they can reason over models, so kept-in-sync models that usefully approximate the system let an agent walk the docs, hit a pointer to the linked model, and make the change with the whole picture in one window.

Which model the agent reaches for shifts with its move — architecture to plan, the module to write, the journey to ask whether the change still serves the user — so the models form a hierarchy, and the craft is meeting each step at the altitude where it is legible; one sweet-spot model cannot give that, a set of honest linked models can.

A model also lets the agent check its work — an invariant over a model says what must be true beyond the tests, so the agent follows the model, verifies against it, and retrofits the map when the territory genuinely moves — and drift-and-parity gates make "the map equals the territory" a checked property that fails the build the moment model and code disagree.

sections.heading_text: Why agents don't reach for models on their own — a conjecture
sections.topic_sentence: Here a skeptic has a fair question.

points.text: An agent's reluctance to reach for models is conjectured to compound two corpus effects — serious model-based engineering hides inside regulated industry and never leaks into the training corpus, and the public text about models is mostly negative — so the agent is conditioned away twice over; its reluctance is an echo of the era that abandoned models for the cost agents just removed, not evidence that models do not help.

sections.heading_text: The apex of the documentation hierarchy is a typed model
sections.topic_sentence: Step back from drift for a moment and look at what you actually hand an agent to work from.

points.text: What you hand an agent is never one thing but a hierarchy of descriptions of intent — prose docs, code comments, tests, schemas — each aimed at the same system from a different angle, and every one of them is partial and drifts: the prose goes stale, the comment outlives its code, the test pins yesterday's behavior, the schema lags the migration.

The usual agentic recipe gives docs, code, and tests but nothing binding them, so they sit as three separate islands: nothing relates them, nothing can tell you they have fallen out of agreement, and drift is therefore not a risk you run but the default you discover only when it bites.

The move is to take the documentation hierarchy to its limit, whose apex is not more prose but a typed model: precise enough that a machine can read it, and because it can, check the other descriptions against it — the one edge that binds docs, code, and tests into a checkable whole and surfaces any disagreement the instant it appears instead of the instant it bites.

The Modeling Thesis at full strength: climb the now-cheap documentation hierarchy all the way to a typed model that binds intent to implementation and a checker can prove things about, because everything below it drifts while the model is the one description that cannot silently lie — the gate stays red until it tells the truth again — which is why the models-bridge earns its own role.

One school stops one rung short by keeping intent in constrained English — requirements written to a strict grammar, a real model reserved for high-stakes cases — but structured English is still prose a checker cannot hold the code up to, and reserving the model for where stakes justify it is the old where-warranted hedge from a world where keeping the map current cost a person's labor, a cost agents removed.

sections.heading_text: A drift check proves agreement, not correctness
sections.topic_sentence: The claim I just made hides a trap, and the book's enthusiasm for drift gates can be misread into a dangerous half-truth.

points.text: A model wired to a drift check cannot rot, but it can still be wrong: the gate proves only that model and code agree, and says nothing about whether either matches what you meant — both can move together in the same wrong direction while the gate stays a contented green.

The power was never in modeling as such but in the model being authored independently of the code: a model derived from the code is a mirror that reflects what is and cannot tell you what it reflects is wrong, while a model authored from intent is a spec that says what ought to be — and only a spec catches a wrong "is," though the drift check looks identical in both cases.

The caveat does not weaken the drift gate; it says what the gate is for: checking that model and code agree is mechanical and automated, but deciding what belongs in the model — which concepts and "ought"s it must carry — does not automate, so it is the essential residual that moves one level up, from writing correct code to authoring the model that says what correct means.

sections.heading_text: Just execute the model? A short history of CASE and MDA
sections.topic_sentence: If the typed model is where you now start, an old idea says to finish there too: skip the code and *execute the model directly*.

points.text: If the typed model is where you now start, an old idea says to finish there too — skip the code and execute the model directly; the field spent forty years on that idea, and where it landed marks the boundary this book keeps.

The dream of executing the model had several names: CASE tools in the 1980s promised round-trip engineering so design and code never diverged, and in 2001 the OMG's Model-Driven Architecture — with Executable UML's action language — went the whole way to "do not write the code, just execute the model."

Executable models failed to take the mainstream less from a tool failure than a mismatch of tempo: Agile-era software changed by the week and heavy modeling could not keep pace, so outside regulated niches the guarantees a model bought were not worth its rigidity, and a survey of practitioners found teams generate key parts through small domain-specific languages, not whole systems.

Read the outcome as a spectrum, not a verdict: from no modeling (fast, no guarantee past the tests) to the executable model that is the system (intent bound tightest, least forgiving of change), every point trades the same way — the further you model, the stronger the result and the harder it is to move — and Brooks guards the far end, since a model never eases essential complexity.

The book takes no strong stance on where to stop because the sweet spot moved and is still moving: a derived gate that keeps the map equal to the territory for almost nothing lets you sit far further along the line than the Agile era could, so the old verdict against executable models is worth reopening, and the book works a comfortable stretch it does not claim is the optimum.

sections.heading_text: The semantic gap
sections.topic_sentence: Enforce a property at the wrong level and it slips through; [ref:semantic-gap] shows the fix — lift the check to where the meaning is legible.

points.text: Enforce a property at the wrong level of abstraction and it slips through; the fix is to lift the check up to where the meaning is legible.

Enforcing "call-graph changed but model not updated, reject it" at the commit sounds like a pre-commit hook but is not one: an agent carrying out a real task makes many commits toward one goal, the model may be legitimately out of sync mid-way and correct by the end, so checking at the commit is checking a sentence for grammar before the paragraph is written.

The semantic gap is the failure you get whenever you enforce a property at the wrong level of abstraction — the same shape as OS security, where "this program is exfiltrating data" is a pattern across many system calls invisible in any single one; model drift at the commit is that shape, the commit being the wrong granularity.

The fix is to enforce at the level where the property is actually legible; for model drift that is the agent returning from its task, when the whole feature and its plan are visible — exactly where a definition-of-done audit runs, over the whole unit of work rather than any single commit, checking that the model was updated and the surrounding work is complete.

sections.heading_text: A worked example: the context-fullness bank-hook
sections.topic_sentence: Let me give you a second instance of the semantic gap, one that lives not in the product but in the operator's own loop.

points.text: When a long session fills the context window the harness compacts — a lossy save whose keep-or-drop decision is a best-effort guess, because the harness sees only tokens and cannot know which parts were load-bearing; only the operator knows what was worth banking, so the harness sits below the semantics of "what is worth keeping" and can only approximate.

sections.heading_text: The fix: a hook one level up, checking two things
sections.topic_sentence: So I moved the check up to where the property *is* legible: the operator's loop.

points.text: The fix is to move the check up to where the property is legible — the operator's loop, at a hook the orchestrator controls — firing on two conditions together: whether the context window is getting full (the harness exposes this) and whether the durable records have gone stale (the part the harness cannot see, a fact about meaning).

sections.heading_text: Why both conditions, and not one
sections.topic_sentence: The dual check is not belt-and-suspenders.

points.text: Firing the reminder on fullness alone nags after every fill even when nothing changed, and firing on staleness alone nags every few minutes; either single loose condition fires too often and trains the operator into the ouroboros — the degenerate state where the model spends its turns summarizing its own recent work instead of doing new work.

sections.heading_text: The honest part: the pre-compact hook is the wrong hook
sections.topic_sentence: I want to be straight about a compromise buried in this, because it is the kind of thing the semantic-gap idea should make you notice rather than paper over.

points.text: The theoretically right moment to bank is the instant before compaction, and the harness offers a pre-compact hook there, but it is the wrong hook: it fires too close to the end to fit a comfortable bank, and worse, the bank itself costs tokens, so a save kicked off at that boundary can be the very thing that trips the compaction it was meant to precede.

Unlike the drift example, where agent-return is genuinely the level at which the property is legible, this case has no clean rung — the harness gives a pre-compact hook too late to use and a fullness number too dumb to act on alone — so the honest choice is a hook at roughly the right level, the operator's loop checking fullness and staleness together, accepting a little loss.

preamble_points.text: The most valuable thing to inject at any layer is a model — the sweet spot between prose too vague and code too verbose — but a model only helps if you check it at a level where checking makes sense, and pushing on it at the wrong level is the trap that catches people the moment they try to enforce one.

sections.heading_text: Ex-ante: everything you can decide up front
sections.topic_sentence: Some things you genuinely know from the beginning, and you should write every one of them down.

points.text: Some things you genuinely know from the beginning — a coding style guide's rules are the everyday example — and you should write every one down and then determinize it with a deterministic check the agent itself can write; this specification-driven development costs almost nothing and gives a much stronger starting point.

sections.heading_text: Ex-post: everything you learn by building
sections.topic_sentence: But you will not know everything, and pretending otherwise is the mistake.

points.text: You will not know everything up front, so you build governance ex-post — after the fact, iteratively, strapping on new mechanisms as failures reveal themselves and the software's real properties emerge — defining what you can in advance and staying willing to discover the rest.

The honest loop is watch it burn and then try to fix it: the failures you did not foresee teach you which mechanism to build next, so ex-post governance is not a fallback for a weak plan but where most real mechanisms come from, because most real failures are the ones no specification predicted.

The engine of the discipline is to hold a quality goal by setting up a mechanism that keeps it — placed up front from what you know, or added in response to a failure seen twice, so yesterday's manually-caught mistake becomes today's automatic check enforced on every agent — and however you arrive, the mechanism takes one of two forms: a firewall or a smoke detector.

sections.heading_text: Constraints and sensors
sections.topic_sentence: A mechanism is one of two moves — prevent the mistake, or catch it — and [ref:constraint-vs-sensor] draws the split.

points.text: A mechanism is one of two moves — prevent the mistake, or catch it — however you arrived at the quality goal it holds.

Words alone do not hold — a prompt raises the odds of the agent following an instruction but never settles them, because it is a probability flip — so instead of hoping you determinize it: check the condition before the agent acts and refuse when it is not met, turning a soft instruction into a hard gate, and that move splits into the two forms below.

A sensor detects drift: it lets the mistake happen and catches it after the fact — a test suite or lint in CI — and because it fires after, it fails the loop iteration and the agent must run again to fix what it caught, so a sensor's cost is iterations, which is why you do not reach for one first.

A sensor is only as good as the signal it can read, and observability is the property that a running system exposes enough signal to explain what it did and catch what went wrong — the wiring under every sensor; build it first and the sensor has something to watch, skip it and it stares at a blank wall.

A constraint prevents drift by scoping the agent's action space within the iteration so the wrong move is never available to pick — a typed enumeration instead of bare strings the model would silently mis-synonym — so the compiler rejects the bad value on the spot; a constraint that removes a mistake costs no iteration, while a sensor that catches it costs at least one.

Two independent axes cross here: a mechanism's form — soft (it aims the agent) or hard (it holds regardless) — and its move — a constraint (it prevents) or a sensor (it detects); constraint-versus-sensor is what the mechanism does, soft-versus-hard is how firmly it does it, and the two are independent.

Most real mechanisms are a package across both axes — a typed model is a soft constraint that ships with hard sensors, the definition-of-done review a constraining runbook wrapped in flagging sensors — so name the package and tag its primary move rather than forcing it into one bin: prefer a constraint where you can build one, add a sensor for the drift you cannot scope away.

A purely organizational answer to an unreliable worker — review, approval, evidence trail, sign-off — is all sensors: each catches the mistake ex-post, an iteration late, so it can shrink the blast radius but never remove a failure class, because it watches the action space instead of scoping it; the constraint is the move that answer does not have.

You place some constraints and sensors up front and add more as you go, and stepping back, that combination — determinize what you can, then convert every recurring surprise into a constraint or a sensor — is the governed engineering environment: policies for how the work should proceed that produce the rules of the road the agents operate within.

sections.heading_text: The residual: goals no mechanism reaches
sections.topic_sentence: That closing line reads as if it settles everything.

points.text: Some goals split into neither a constraint nor a sensor: no cheap sensor can see the failure and no constraint can scope it away, because the failure is an absence nobody specified — and you cannot watch for the violation of a rule no one wrote or forbid an action the design never mentioned.

Security remediation is the clean case: a missing authorization check has no failing test by definition, because a caught gap was a specified one, so the goal stays a human job — someone must know the check should be there — and this residual, the third outcome beside prevent and detect, runs at your speed while the mechanized goals run at fleet speed, so it, not the size of the catalogue, bounds the whole system.

The residual is not the soft end of the soft-versus-hard axis: a soft mechanism is still a named artifact you can point to and add to the census, while the residual has nothing to name, nothing to tag as constraint or sensor — it is the complement of the two moves, not a third value on the axis.

Naming the residual is not a weakness in the method — a method that claims to mechanize everything is the one to distrust — it is the honest edge that says plainly what the catalogue does not cover, and that admission is what lets you trust the coverage it does claim.

The residual is not a fixed wall: you can pull a goal out by authoring the missing spec — the same absence that defeats a sensor defeats a derived model (a mirror cannot see what was never specified) and greens a journey test that only asserts the flow ran, until a human authors the terminal task-closure assertion that says what done means, turning an un-sensable goal into a checkable post-condition.

preamble_points.text: Because you discover what you are building by building part of it, you cannot specify everything up front, so a governed environment has two halves — what you can decide before you start and what you can only learn along the way — and every governance mechanism finally takes one of two forms.

sections.heading_text: Lifecycles first, then the failure map
sections.topic_sentence: Start with the lifecycles, because everything else hangs off them.

points.text: Start with the lifecycles, because everything hangs off them: a lifecycle is the correct operation of one recurring activity — how a bug moves from filed to fixed, a feature from design to shipped — so write the healthy path first, then from each node map the ways it can go wrong and, for each, the action to take, a grid of every node crossed with every symptom.

Building that grid is failure mode and effects analysis: enumerate what can go wrong, the consequence of each, and — the part people skip — how to get out of it; you know the way out (reconcile a conflict by reading both sides' intent, wipe the fat cache when the disk fills) but the agent knows none of it and may reach for something catastrophic, so coach it on where the hot points are and, in every failure path, what is not allowed — encoding the prohibition as a mechanism at the right level where you can, and stating it plainly where you cannot.

Naming a forbidden act can plant the temptation — the pink-elephant problem — so a bare prohibition can backfire and, worse, leaves the agent stuck with nowhere to go when the forbidden lever was its only escape; what works is pairing the forbidden move with the sanctioned one that reaches the same goal safely, so the rule reads "not that lever, this one" and replaces the temptation instead of merely raising it.

sections.heading_text: Runbooks: split the deterministic from the judgment
sections.topic_sentence: Once the healthy path and the failure map are written, the thing you hand the agent is a **runbook** (or playbook): the steps to take, whether recovering from a failure or working a fresh ticket.

points.text: Once the healthy path and the failure map are written, the thing you hand the agent is a runbook — the steps to take, recovering from a failure or working a fresh ticket — and the one discipline that makes it work is to split it into two kinds of step, deterministic and judgment, because the two are governed completely differently.

The deterministic parts get tools: anything with a single correct outcome should be an executable script the agent runs, not a procedure it improvises — improvisation gets it right most of the time, and you will wish you had automated it the one time it does not.

Determinizing a step buys more than a reliable outcome — it buys a trace: the inputs read, the branch taken, the value produced, written down in a fixed shape instead of vanishing as an improvised step's smoke, and that record has two consumers — the next turn of the loop, which starts from what was already reasoned instead of re-deriving it, and a second checker that reads the trace to audit how the answer was reached and flag a path it should not have taken.

sections.heading_text: The judgment parts: the roughest algorithm that still fits
sections.topic_sentence: **The judgment parts get the roughest algorithm that still fits.** For a well-constrained decision, write the algorithm down and let the agent do the glue.

points.text: The judgment parts get the roughest algorithm that still fits: write the algorithm down for a well-constrained decision, but for an open-ended one — a threat hunt whose premise is that the attacker did something unanticipated — do not over-constrain, because you are conditioning a probability distribution and steering it down the wrong path means it never reaches the answer, so give hints where you have them, say "solve this open-endedly" where you truly do not, and accept that looser guidance spends more tokens and lands less often.

When a judgment step is really a measurement, give it a rubric: you cannot write a checker for "is this painting good," but you can operationalize the question into gradable parts — topic sentences, technique, grammatical errors, storage blotches — and the agent, though it will not deliver a verdict on taste, returns feedback good enough to act on.

The strongest form is the pre-canned brief: when an orchestrator hands work to a sub-agent you do not want it re-inventing how to explain the task each time, so you give it a template it adapts — the work already articulated — and a brief-linter that checks the template is intact before launch, which applies the book's whole business of constraining how work is described to agents to the act of delegation itself.

preamble_points.text: An agent knows how to commit to Git but not the life cycles of your engineered environment — what to do when the disk fills, when two branches conflict, when an incident pages at 2 a.m. — because it has no operating context and no sense of how you do things, so a governed environment for real work must write that operational judgment down as lifecycles and the runbooks that ride on them.

sections.heading_text: Measure one level deeper
sections.topic_sentence: John Ousterhout gives the rule in one line: **measure one level deeper than the number you think you want.** A metric earns its place only when it drives a decision, and the surface number usually cannot.

points.text: Ousterhout's rule in one line — measure one level deeper than the number you think you want — because a metric earns its place only when it drives a decision, and the surface number usually cannot.

A cloud bill is real and useless: it tells you to pay the invoice, not what to change — but split the same bill by service and one usually dominates while the rest trail off in a thin tail, and the dominant one names your first target, the deeper number carrying a decision the shallow one buried.

An 8-second boot as one number means only "scale out"; measured one level deeper — 6 of those seconds are one initialization phase warming up — it means "optimize that phase first," the same latency turned from a reflexive scale-out into a specific engineering decision.

The same trap hides in test coverage: "the suite covers 87% of lines" is the invoice-level headline that reports and does not act, because a line in a throwaway helper counts the same as a line in the job state machine, so the chapter's flagship metric is coverage measured one level deeper — coverage that names the gap instead of hiding it in a percentage.

The metric spectrum tracks the soft-versus-hard governance axis: a hard metric is deterministic — a machine reads it and the same input yields the same number — while a soft metric is judgment-laden, pointing a reader at a place to look without reducing to a self-deciding threshold; both are worth having, and the mistake is to treat one as the other — blocking a build on a soft signal, or leaving a hard fact to a reviewer's memory.

sections.heading_text: The hard end: cold-start latency, machine-read and model-fed
sections.topic_sentence: Start at the deterministic end, where a metric is a millisecond number nobody argues about.

points.text: A serverless fleet scales to zero, so a request that wakes a cold instance waits while the container boots and the runtime loads — the cold-start latency — and the obvious reading is the penalty of scaling from zero: measure it, and if it hurts, pay to keep a warm instance running.

The obvious reading was wrong: a validator service carried a multi-second warm floor a warm instance did nothing to remove, and the deeper number named its cause — a runtime relaunched once per request paying a fresh startup each time — so the fix was a re-architecture that kept the runtime resident, cutting the warm floor many-fold; the barrier was runtime initialization, not scale-from-zero and not image size, and only the deeper measurement said so.

Spot-checking the one service whose latency looked wrong does not scale — it catches the service that draws your eye and says nothing about how services interact — so the better instrument is a model holding every service's numbers and reasoning over the paths between them, because the sharpest question is the chain: a request landing when every downstream service is cold triggers a cascade, and the worst case is a longest-path sum, each step contributing the slowest cold-start it waits on.

The hard end's defining move is that the number feeds the model: the cold-start measurements do not live in a dashboard a human reads and forgets — they land as typed fields on the deployment-topology model the fleet reasons through, and a recompute tool reads those fields to derive the longest-path worst case, refining on its own whenever a fresher number is written.

The commit is automated because a runbook step — "after a measurement run, remember to commit the new numbers" — rots and the model drifts; so the pipeline commits the refreshed measurements itself under a housekeeping commit with no human in the loop, building the map's upkeep into the machine that changes the territory rather than asking a person to remember it: architecture over a reminder.

As-built, the live-annotation path is built but not yet populated — the tool runs off a snapshot table of measured values because the fleet is mid-migration — which is the ordinary shape of real work, the seam in and the data catching up; what matters for the chapter is the pattern: a hard metric measured deterministically, written into a typed model, and consumed by a tool that turns it into a decision.

sections.heading_text: The flagship: coverage measured one level deeper
sections.topic_sentence: Now the middle of the spectrum, and the chapter's teaching example: the "measure one level deeper" rule applied to the number that most often gets it wrong.

points.text: Line coverage answers a syntactic question — did this line run under some test — which is useful but cannot answer the engineer's actual, semantic question: is the claim this code makes exercised by a test? A file can sit at 95% while the one function implementing a critical invariant is never called, its lines covered incidentally by an unrelated test, so the percentage is true and also a lie about the thing you care about, and the lie is invisible because a percentage has nowhere to put the gap.

The fix joins two things the system already has: a traceability graph linking each model claim — an invariant, a transition, a service-flow edge — to the code that implements it, pointing at an anchor (the entry-point symbol that carries the claim), and the ordinary coverage oracle that knows which source lines ran; compose them — anchor to its symbol's line range, intersected with the covered-line set — and you can ask whether this claim's code was exercised.

The composition changes the unit of measurement: line coverage counts lines, this counts model claims — the anchors supply the numerator's units, coverage supplies the ground truth of what ran — so the metric reports not a percentage but a named verdict ("this invariant's implementing code is not exercised by any test"), turning an anonymous 87% into an actionable list of the exact model claims the suite walks past.

Run the genre check and this metric has a name — requirements-based coverage, the discipline avionics certification mandates and an open-source requirements tool encodes with git-native items linked to their tests — so the work is not to dream up a bespoke number but to compute the known figure over a graph already built for it, adding the one synthesis the off-the-shelf tools lack: they check a requirement has a linked test, not that the linked test actually executes the requirement's code.

One primitive underneath — resolve an anchor to a line range and intersect it with the covered set — supports several aggregations, each answering a different decision: model-element coverage (which claims that anchor real code go unexercised, the headline fix-list), entry-point coverage (which anchored roots a refactor regression would slip past), and chain coverage (does each claim close end-to-end — code, a test naming it as verifier, and that test actually running the code — the strictest cut that reports low at first and thereby names the verification chains still to build).

The honesty layer matters as much as the aggregation: a single percentage lies when its denominator is fuzzy, so every figure reports a breakdown — exercised, not-exercised, unmeasurable (anchor unresolvable), out-of-surface (legitimately not coverable code) — and "80%" then reads as what it is, a number that affords the engineering because you can see which part of it you can act on.

The design is deliberately light: computing all of this requires no change to any model — the anchors already carry their symbol, the covered-line set is a plain read of the coverage database — so the metric is a new consumer of two existing substrates whose expensive parts were already paid for, and measuring one level deeper cost a join, not a rebuild.

sections.heading_text: The soft end: doc-derived tests
sections.topic_sentence: Slide to the far end of the spectrum, where the metric stops being a number a threshold can act on and becomes a judgment a human has to make.

points.text: A doc-derived test pins a behavior stated in a cited document, carrying a trailer that names its source so an edit to the source regenerates the pin; the metric it invites — is this doc-claim pinned by a test? — is genuinely soft, with no clean denominator, because "how many claims does this document make?" is a matter of reading (one reader finds six, another nine, neither wrong) and the set of claims is not enumerable by machine, so the signal points a reader at a document and says "these deserve a pin," it does not decide.

The softness runs deeper than a fuzzy denominator: a doc-derived test is only as good as the seam it tests against, so if decision logic is interleaved with live I/O there is no pure surface to assert against and the test falls back to pinning the source's shape — a test that stays green even when you gut the function's body — which makes the signal inseparable from a judgment about readiness that only a human can answer, and wiring it to a gate that blocks on a threshold manufactures exactly the hollow tests it was meant to prevent.

sections.heading_text: The model runs the machinery
sections.topic_sentence: The hard end and the flagship follow the same pattern.

points.text: The models are not documentation that merely stays in sync with the code — they are consumed at runtime to produce the metrics: the cold-start numbers are typed fields a tool reads to derive the longest-path worst case, and the coverage flagship walks the traceability graph to each claim's anchor rather than scanning source for important-looking functions, so in both the model is not a picture of the machinery, it is the machinery — the thing the metric tool reads to know what to measure and how to weigh it.

The sharpest instance ties metrics back to mechanisms: a pre-commit gate deciding whether a lint finding should block grades each finding by its distance from the change in the typed component graph — HARD on a touched file (block, the commit's own debt), SOFT in the same component (report and ask, do not block, so concurrent agents do not race the same pre-existing problem), SILENT in a different component (suppress, leaving the whole-tree deploy gate as backstop).

The grade is a metric — a distance read from the model at check time — that drives a sensor's decision directly: the same finding gets three gate behaviors, chosen by consulting the component graph about how far it sits from the change, so here the model is not describing the system for a human to read later, it is queried at the moment of commit to grade the gate — the machinery, run by the model.

sections.heading_text: A compact reference
sections.topic_sentence: [ref:metrics-table] collects every metric — the decision each drives, where it sits on the hard-soft axis, and who reads it.

points.text: Read the table top to bottom and the spectrum is visible at a glance — stopwatch-hard machine-consumed rows at the top, a hard measurement turned onto a semantic unit in the middle, a reader-aiming judgment at the bottom — and every row names a decision, because a metric that names no decision was measured too shallow, and a loop steering by a shallow number is a loop that cannot steer.

preamble_points.text: Every agent runs a loop — input, reason, act, fold the result back around — and this chapter develops the sensing half of it, because a loop with no honest sense of its own state cannot steer at all.

A metric senses, a playbook acts, a mechanism enforces — and the metric comes first because the other two are blind without it: a playbook firing on the wrong number does the wrong work, a mechanism grading on too coarse a number blocks the wrong commit, so the governing question for every metric is not "can I measure this?" but "does this number drive a decision?"

sections.heading_text: Drawing what lies between the controls
sections.topic_sentence: The Governance Graph draws it.

points.text: The Governance Graph draws the space between controls: nodes are the mechanisms, each tagged with the event it fires on and the resources it reads, writes, or locks, and edges are the conflicts in a closed four-value taxonomy — contradiction, contention, ordering, and soft-versus-hard — joined by the shared resource rather than any call, so two controls that never call each other still collide if they touch the same slot, and typing the turn-end slot and the context budget as resources brings hook-pileup and injection-pressure under the same machinery as a contended lock.

The shared resource is what lets the graph reason across lifecycles: a turn-end hook and a commit-time check live in different lifecycles but still collide if they reach for one typed resource, and the resource is the only coupling surface between lifecycles — controls that share none cannot conflict, which keeps the graph sparse — and this is the semantic gap again, the collision a property of the interaction, invisible in either control's own code and legible only at the level where both are drawn.

A catalogue lists the controls but cannot show which two will crash; the graph draws exactly those crashes — the edges a list of nodes omits, the static catalogue's dynamic dual — and the answer splits cleanly: mechanically decidable edges (a same-slot pair with no declared order, a lock cycle) route to a sensor a lint settles, while semantic edges (are two demands on a commit-set truly incompatible, or do they compose?) route to a human prompt, so each edge carries its nature derived from its type and both the flag and the prompt land before the control ships, not at the collision.

The operational payoff: a governed environment is not just a pile of running mechanisms but a claim that they compose — a claim that was implicit, checked only by collision — and the graph makes it explicit and checkable, answering at authoring time "what fires on this event, what touches this resource, is this new control consistent with the ones already wired," so the fleet stops merely running its guardrails and starts modeling how they interact.

sections.heading_text: When the hooks aren't yours
sections.topic_sentence: Every mechanism so far was one you wrote.

points.text: Every mechanism so far was one you wrote, but some hooks arrive from outside — a plugin, a teammate, and plausibly soon a regulator or model vendor mandating "run your agents with these prescribed governance hooks or fall out of compliance" — and the graph extends to these without changing shape.

An outside hook enters as a node with its firing event known but its resource footprint unknown — and unknown is not empty, since empty would mean "verified to touch nothing" — so it sits on a possible-conflict edge against every mechanism sharing its slot until someone analyzes it into a known node, and that conservative default is the honest reading of a black box, creating the right pressure: an unreconciled mandated hook shows up as unresolved conflict, never as silent trust.

The graph becomes a substrate for composing governance you did not author: satisfying one regulator is checking that your mechanisms plus theirs leave no unresolved conflict, satisfying several is the same check over the union, and because the graph types soft-versus-hard it can settle the property a mandate cares about most — that a required hard block is never quietly overridden by one of your soft aims on the same slot — so "do I satisfy all of them at once?" becomes a question the model answers at authoring time instead of at audit.

sections.heading_text: Keeping the model honest
sections.topic_sentence: Two disciplines keep the model honest, and both are the book's.

points.text: Two disciplines keep the model honest: anchor each node to the code that implements its control by symbol, never by line, so a drift lint re-resolves the anchor every build and a control wired but unmodeled reddens the gate; and keep the model descriptive — it draws the controls that exist and checks proposed ones on request, it does not invent conflict-lints for collisions that never happened — because a governance graph is itself a governance mechanism, and the failure mode of governance is a tower nobody wants.

preamble_points.text: The stack gives four layers to steer at and a governed fleet fills them with accumulating constraints, each earning its place alone; but together they form a system, and a system of controls has the one failure a list of controls cannot show — two of them making incompatible demands on the same thing at the same moment.

Two collisions from the case study make it concrete — a squashed-commit requirement colliding with an out-of-brief check on the same commit-set, and two turn-end hooks firing with no order declared between them — and neither lives in any one control's code: each lives in the space between two controls, two correct controls making a contradictory demand on one shared resource, a space drawn nowhere until the graph draws it.

sections.heading_text: The expense that buried MBSE is the one a fleet pays for free
sections.topic_sentence: Model-based systems engineering never failed on its ideas.

points.text: Model-based systems engineering never failed on its ideas; it failed on its upkeep — keeping a hand-drawn model matched to a moving codebase is dull, unending human work, the first thing a deadline cuts, so the diagrams drifted, then lied, then got ignored.

Re-inducing a model from the code, diffing it, regenerating what it feeds is exactly the dull, unending upkeep a fleet does for nearly nothing — so the one expense that buried MBSE is the one thing an agent fleet supplies cheaply, and the map stays equal to the territory because keeping it equal now costs almost nothing.

The move is to stop listing kinds of model and start walking them; reconciled with the general model types a systems-engineering course teaches, the real drift-checked zoo is large enough that one model is never the whole picture — which is exactly Kruchten's thesis about architecture.

MBSE here means software: the models are typed records, state machines, and the code's own structures, borrowing SysML's words where they name something but refusing its usual form of a model drawn beside the code — a second representation is a snapshot that drifts — and it stops at discrete software, since continuous or real-time dynamics want the timed and hybrid automata toolkit instead.

Working at the model level with an agent doing the lifting buys three things a team usually trades against each other — fewer tokens, more velocity, higher quality, together — because a model shrinks what the agent must hold in-window; that combination is the shape Brooks called a silver bullet, and the careful claim is that the model level is the closest thing to one, since it changes the representation the agent reasons over rather than promising to make the hard part easy.

sections.heading_text: Data from the case study
sections.topic_sentence: The fewer-tokens leg is the one we can measure directly.

points.text: The fewer-tokens leg is the one measured directly: in a controlled A/B pilot an agent answered four navigation questions about the modeled codebase with the model-navigation guidance loaded and without it, and the tokens each arm spent were counted.

The median saving is about −35% at zero accuracy loss — every modeled arm answered correctly on and off, so the guidance bought cheaper answers rather than different ones — and the saving scales with how much derivation the naive path would otherwise have had to redo.

sections.heading_text: Kruchten's 4+1, promoted from a closing sentence to the spine
sections.topic_sentence: The last chapter invoked Kruchten's **4+1 views** in a final sentence — "the reason one model is never enough." This Part promotes that sentence to its organizing structure.

points.text: This Part promotes Kruchten's 4+1 from a closing sentence to its organizing structure: no single diagram captures a software architecture, so four complementary views — logical, process, development, physical — plus a fifth, the scenarios that validate them, cover what a working engineer needs to see.

sections.heading_text: What this book adds to 4+1: the drift gate
sections.topic_sentence: Kruchten described the views.

points.text: This book's contribution on top of 4+1 is the drift gate: every view here is not a diagram a human maintains but a typed model a tool reads on every build, gated to fail the moment model and code disagree — 4+1 says which views you need, the drift gate keeps each from becoming a diagram that rots.

sections.heading_text: The framework is a choice; the core is not
sections.topic_sentence: Making the model executable is why this Part is not really *about* 4+1.

points.text: Once the core is a typed model held equal to the code, a view framework is a projection over that core, not a second thing you maintain — you keep one executable model and render whatever view-set the audience needs from it, which is why this Part is not really about 4+1.

Change the audience and you change the projection, not the model: the Process view, a C4 Context-and-Container view, SysML constraint blocks, a data-flow diagram look like rival methodologies but are renderings of the same structure, and a system whose core is executable can derive any of them.

The same move works one level finer: even inside a single framework a view must choose what to show, and that choice is a second projection kept honest by a clean split — the content is a pure function of the source models, authored by no one, while the lens picks which content a view shows and may hide a node but can never invent one, so even the customer's slice cannot drift from the truth.

This Part teaches modeling, not a modeling framework: it uses 4+1 as a good spine for an engineer's questions and drift-gates each view on real code, but the transferable claim sits one level up — hit the executable core and the framework wars dissolve into projection choices, so choose the core with care and choose the framework and lens to fit the reader.

sections.heading_text: The trunk: machinery that holds any view true
sections.topic_sentence: Before the views, one chapter of framing.

points.text: Most of the method models belong to no single view — they are the trunk machinery that makes every view executable and drift-proof: the executable source-of-truth, the drift and parity gates, the agent-first harness, and the read-and-generate surfaces — introduced once here and revisited by each view chapter.

sections.heading_text: Beat 1 — a model is derived and joined, never repeated
sections.topic_sentence: The last chapter warned against repetition: two models that say the same thing must now be kept in sync.

points.text: The zoo's organizing rule sharpens the last chapter's warning against repetition: a model here never sits beside the code as a parallel document — it is derived from the code, or the code from it, and it joins to its neighbours on a shared key rather than restating them.

Concretely: the service-flow model is not a re-listing of the endpoints but the list the access policy is generated from and the call graph is checked against, and a journey model joins to those endpoints by call-site rather than copying them — so repetition is the failure and derivation-plus-join is the cure.

sections.heading_text: Beat 2 — name the direction of derivation
sections.topic_sentence: A model and the code it concerns stay equal by derivation, and derivation runs in one of two directions.

points.text: A model and the code it concerns stay equal by derivation, and that derivation runs in one of two directions — model-from-code (induce and reconcile) or model-to-code (specify and generate); say which up front, because the gate machinery differs between them.

Most models in the zoo run model-from-code, because the codebase pre-existed the models; the service-flow model is the clearest model-to-code case and is bidirectional — some fields generated to code, others reconciled from it — which is why its gate checks both directions.

sections.heading_text: Beat 3 — every model traces to the code
sections.topic_sentence: A model earns trust only if you can get from a model element back to the lines that realize it, and forward from a line to the model element that governs it.

points.text: A model earns trust only through a round-trip — from a model element back to the lines that realize it, and forward from a line to the element that governs it — and that round-trip is traceability, exactly what the safety-critical standards demanded and exactly what the drift gate's reconciler mechanizes on every build.

Traceability is why the per-model template folds a one-line note into each page — the direction the model derives and the join key from a model row back to the code — so a reader always knows how to round-trip from the picture to the lines.

The whole zoo rests on the round-trip: a set of views earns trust only while every view still tracks the code it depicts, and a drifted view misleads every agent that reasons through it, so a zoo of drifted views is worse than none because it lends false confidence — and Kruchten gave the views but never said how one stays equal to the code under hundreds of authors and a fleet rewriting the territory daily.

The answer defended here is that the round-trip must itself be derived, not snapshotted: write the traceability graph's edges down once and trust them and it is a frozen snapshot that drifts the first time a symbol it names is deleted, but give each edge the mechanism that re-proves it — resolve the target against the code and see whether it still exists — and a deletion turns the edge red, because a check that re-reads the code cannot fall behind it while a stored copy can.

The derived graph pays a second dividend: because a resolving edge means the map is current, an agent can walk it to pull the slice of a codebase it cannot hold in one window — up to the invariant that governs a line, down to the code that realizes it — so the systems model a senior engineer keeps in their head becomes a navigable index the fleet reasons through, and drift-detection and navigation are one property wearing two faces.

sections.heading_text: Keeping the models honest — the traceability substrate
sections.topic_sentence: DocAble did not design this up front.

points.text: This substrate was not designed up front: DocAble tried the cheaper approach first, watched it fail on real work, and built the substrate from what broke — a story worth walking because it shows the exact shape a snapshot rots into and why a derived edge does not.

A model is only as good as its agreement with the code: let it still describe a poll-based dispatch plane after a serverless push plane has replaced it and every agent that trusts the model plans against a system that no longer exists — the map must equal the territory, or the map lies.

The tempting fix — a checklist to update the model whenever a subsystem is retired — fails the way it always fails: a cutover reconciled the docs and the agent boot context but forgot the models, and the forgotten edge stayed green because nothing re-checked it, which is the pattern under every silent drift — a hand-maintained list rots the moment the code moves without it, unnoticed until the stale fact bites.

sections.heading_text: Reading the fix off real drift
sections.topic_sentence: The right sensor was not guessed.

points.text: The right sensor was not guessed: the models were left deliberately ungoverned for weeks so the fix could be read off real drift, and an audit of the closed work turned up two dozen silent divergences at a signal-to-noise near one — sorted by what caught them, one line separated clean from drifted, the clean ones having a sensor that re-read the code at check time and the drifted ones a hand-maintained second copy of the fact that fell behind.

So DocAble keeps not a checklist but a traceability graph whose every edge is derived — re-checked against the code at scan time rather than trusted from the last look — its nodes being things the system already has (a model element, the lint that enforces it, the code entry point that realizes it, the test that verifies it, a registry row, a doc surface) and its edges the joins between them, each carrying the mechanism that re-proves it: run the resolver against the target and see whether the symbol still exists.

sections.heading_text: Two decisions that make the graph resist rot

points.text: The sensor that walks the graph runs at a slower cadence than the per-commit gates on purpose — resolving a symbol against the code costs far more than the membership lookups a commit hook can afford — so the derived-edge check fires at review and done-checking time, the cadence following the cost, with a cheaper second guard on the anchors themselves catching the case a symbol walk cannot: a pointer left naming a dead implementation while a replacement was built beside it.

This is the one-typed-model-per-format commitment lifted one level up: there a fix through the single seam holds for every format, and here a model stays true because the join to the code is re-derived rather than remembered — a sensor that reads the source of truth at check time cannot fall behind it, while a hand-maintained copy of the same fact always can, so derived sensors defend and snapshotted ones drift.

sections.heading_text: How to read a model page
sections.topic_sentence: Every model in this Part is rendered by filling the same five-field template.

points.text: Every model in this Part is rendered by filling the same five-field template, and the uniformity is deliberate: a reader who has read one page can read any of them on reflex.

The first four fields map onto the four questions a reader brings to a model — what is it for, what is it made of, what does it look like, how do I trust it — and field (e) answers the fifth this chapter raised, how the model stays tied to the code, so each view chapter opens with the Kruchten view it embodies and then walks its models through this template.

preamble_points.text: This Part cashes the last chapter's promise: it walks each kind of model on real code, with real invariants, and shows how to keep the code from drifting away from them.

Under every model in this Part is one real codebase — the production accessibility service the book runs on — carrying dozens of typed, drift-checked models and using everything in the book to stay coherent.

sections.heading_text: The service-flow / API model
sections.topic_sentence: *The typed source-of-truth for a service-oriented architecture — its services, their endpoints, their authentication, and the wiring between them — from which the access policy and environment wiring are generated and against which the real call graph is checked.*

sections.heading_text: The domain registries
sections.topic_sentence: The domain registries are the frozen tables the service-flow model rests on: the file types the system handles, its known conformance gaps, its scheduled jobs, its user-facing surfaces.

sections.heading_text: Formal invariant verification
sections.topic_sentence: Formal invariant verification is the backbone the other three models hang their invariant tables on.

sections.heading_text: The synchronization model
sections.topic_sentence: *A typed registry that models the system's synchronization behavior — every OS-level lock, which shared resource it guards, and the required acquisition ordering — so concurrency contracts are declared and checkable, not tribal.*

sections.heading_text: Two ways to make a concurrent write safe: the mediator and the single-writer registries
sections.topic_sentence: The synchronization model catalogs the raw locks.

sections.heading_text: The mediator registry
sections.topic_sentence: The mediator registry is the *how-many* half.

sections.heading_text: The single-writer registry
sections.topic_sentence: The single-writer registry is the *exactly-one* half, and its failure mode is what makes it a separate model.

sections.heading_text: The component & zone model
sections.topic_sentence: *A typed catalog of every component's code zone — its focus directories, its tags, its boundary kind, its external seams, its read surfaces — so "which component owns this file, and what may touch it" is a queried fact rather than a per-tool guess.*

sections.heading_text: The rule-metadata registry
sections.topic_sentence: The rule-metadata registry is the self-referential slice of the domain registries: the governance rules' own metadata, and so the model the governance substrate — and this book — are partly governed by.

sections.heading_text: The performance/cost view: mostly embodied, one honest gap
sections.topic_sentence: The zoo names a performance and cost model as a general type, and the framework supports it.

sections.heading_text: The deployment & tier topology model
sections.topic_sentence: *The typed statement of where things run — each service's name, its layer, and its tier — from which the deploy scripts and layering lints reason about a declared topology rather than scattered constants, and against which the real deploy table is reconciled.*

sections.heading_text: The invariant-DAG execution policy
